newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Borchert vows to fight farm reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Borchert vows to fight farm reform plan.

text.p: German agriculture minister Jochen Borchert on Thursday said he found new European farm reform plans unacceptable and would demand major alterations.

"We're not trying to postpone problem-solving in EU agriculture, but we are against attempts to tackle problems that don't even exist," he told a briefing on the European Commission proposal, Agenda 2000.
"Most EU member states feel the same way," he added.
Borchert said he would consult his EU colleagues and farm ministers of the 15 German states over the summer.
He would bring to EU farm council meetings in September a detailed set of alternative proposals to Agenda 2000, which was presented by EU Commission president Jacques Santer on Wednesday.

These would focus on securing higher compensation payments to farmers to offset losses from planned support price cuts and to ensure eastern European countries underwent long transition periods before fully joining the EU farm system.
German farmers stood to lose 15 to 20 percent of their incomes if dairy, cereals and beef intervention prices were cut by 10, 20 and 30 percent respectively by 2006 as planned.
Reform of the milk and grains markets should be far less aggressive because there was no threat of fresh surpluses.
The beef sector, on the other hand, needed immediate moves, separate from the price-cutting plans of Agenda 2000, to rid itself of public stocks accumulated in the crisis over mad cow disease.
Agenda 2000 was too quick to abandon successful elements of the EU's 1992 farm reform such as a flexible system of grain intervention coupled with land set-aside and area aid.
Agenda 2000 plans to shift the emphasis from crop-specific price support to direct payments, but higher area aid will not fully offset cuts in intervention prices.
Borchert said this could decouple grain production from the market and make farmers more dependent on state hand-outs.

With grain demand forecast to rise and yields probably not expanding as fast as previously thought, Borchert believed the current system would support grain prices enough to prevent massive export subsidies at the taxpayer's expense.
If that developed, the EU could quickly return to higher land set-aside to stem overproduction.
Oilseed producers needed higher payments than proposed in the single area aid payments which threatened their survival.
Borchert also believed beef intervention price cuts after 2000 would not automatically boost consumption.
The EU should quickly seek to bring supply and demand into balance by reducing livestock numbers eligible for premiums and by subsidising exports, he said.
Dairy support prices should not be cut because quotas were in place to limit production, but better marketing was needed.
EU expansion to embrace the farm sectors of five new eastern European entrants should be slow, perhaps taking eight to 10 years as in the case of Spain and Portugal.
Borchert said Agenda 2000 would worsen Germany's position as a net contributor to the EU.
He also rejected the relaxation of food import rules in the EU ahead of new World Trade Organisation negotiations if this brought in products which did not conform to EU hygiene and safety rules.
The EU upholds a controversial import ban on hormone beef.
